LOS ANGELES (CN) â The Trump administration on Friday dropped its lawsuit to force California election officials to sequester ballots from as many as 20,000 voters on a Homeland Security list of purported noncitizens.

The Justice Department filed a notice of voluntary dismissal in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles after repeatedly failing to get an unprecedented injunction to interfere in how states handle their election procedures.

“In an effort to protect American voters and to prevent the irreparable harm of state and local election officials including illegally cast votes in the final vote tabulation, the United States exhausted its appeals to obtain timely relief all the way to Supreme Court,” the Justice Department said.

“In light of the Supreme Courtâs denial, the United States is evaluating how to best ensure that American votes are protected, including by preventing vote dilution by noncitizens,” the government added.

The voluntary dismissal avoids a hearing scheduled next Friday before U.S. District Judge David Carter on the administration’s bid for a preliminary injunction.

The judge, a Bill Clinton appointee, appointed a special master to help him, before this hearing, get to the bottom of how Homeland Security assembled the disputed list of noncitizens on California voter rolls.

Carter didn’t pull his punches last week when he rejected the Justice Department’s request for a temporary restraining order â a short term legal remedy â to disrupt the counting of mail-in ballots just days before Election Day.

âNever before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch,âÂ Carter said. âIn bringing this lawsuit, the executive would have this court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too.â

The governmentâs request, the judge added,Â violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating states have control over their elections. IfÂ thisÂ last-minute request were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process, he said.

In addition, CarterÂ questioned the credibility of the list of purported noncitizens on Californiaâs voter rolls that Homeland Security compiled, noting a similar list of ineligible voters in Nevada that started with about 16,000 names whittled down to just 185 registered voters who all turned out to be citizens.

Days after Carter’s ruling, the Ninth Circuit in a split decision siding with him.

âWe decline the United Statesâ invitation to contravene the elections clause by undermining the Constitutionâs plain text,â the panel wrote then in a per curiam opinion. âIf the United States believes different procedures are necessary for vote-by-mail ballots, we believe it should take that suggestion to Congress, not the courts.â

While U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett, a Donald Trump appointee, and U.S. Circuit Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Joe Biden appointee, denied the governmentâs appeal, U.S. Circuit Judge Bumatay, also a Trump appointee, dissented, as he had done in the previous ruling.

âThroughout history, federal courts have acted to protect the voting and civil rights of our citizens by enjoining state action that violates the law,â Bumatay wrote. âAnd common sense also tells us that the federal government shouldnât have to sit on its hands while a state allows the violation of federal law, especially when the integrity of federal elections is at stake.â

The U.S. Supreme Court summarily rejected the Trumpâs administration emergency request to interfere in California’s election without even requiring a response from the state. The justices did not explain their decision and there were no noted dissents.

In a statement, Jill Habig, founder and CEO of the Public Rights Project, called the dismissal a victory for all local elections officials.

#7611. Court leans toward narrow ruling on inmate’s use of habeas for accelerated transfer to a halfway house or home confinement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court heard oral argument on Nov. 2 in Maxwell v. Dinis about whether a federal inmate may use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

Maxwell, a former attorney, was convicted at trial for his role in conspiring with a mob-related organization, La Costa Nostra, to take over a Texas-based mortgage-loan company, FirstPlus Financial Group, Inc., and drain it of its assets. As Maxwell neared the end of his sentence, he sought to contest the BOP’s calculation of good-time credits that would accelerate his transfer from prison to a halfway house or home confinement. The question for the court was whether Section 2241, which does not clearly spell out what claims may be brought but whose scope has largely been shaped by precedent, allows him to do so.

Maxwell’s attorney, Masha Hansford, pressed for a broad rule that habeas is available to an inmate like Maxwell who is asserting a right to a “distinct and lower level of custody.” But that position almost immediately encountered some pushback. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson questioned “whether we really need to use this case to define every circumstance in which habeas is appropriate.” Hansford agreed that the court need not adopt a test that allows inmates to challenge all changes to the level of custody and was content to have the court resolve Maxwell’s case by applying a narrower test endorsed by the government that would permit an inmate to use habeas to challenge the denial of an accelerated transfer to parole or, as here, a halfway house or home confinement.

Justice Samuel Alito pressed Hansford on whether an inmate may use Section 2241 simply to dispute how BOP calculated good-time credits or whether the inmate must also show that any error in calculating would also entitle the inmate to accelerated transfer to a halfway house or home confinement. After Hansford replied that Maxwell met all the requirements for the transfer and only the calculation of good-time credits was at issue, Justice Neal Gorsuch followed up by pressing whether the court needs to say that an inmate could bring a habeas challenge about the calculation of good-time credits alone. Hansford replied that the court did not need to say a dispute over good-time credits alone would suffice for a federal inmate to bring a claim in Section 2241.

Turning to Hansford’s level-of-custody test, Justice Sonia Sotomayor noted that, in a prior case, Justice Antonin Scalia had referred to habeas as covering a “‘quantum change’ in the level of custody,” but Hansford was asking the court “to create new language, ‘materially less restrictive custody.’ Why don’t we stick to what we have?” Hansford agreed that the court need not broaden its test and that Maxwell’s requested transfer to a halfway house or home confinement amounted to such a quantum change.

Assistant to the Solicitor General Kevin J. Barber, arguing for the government, contended that “there’s no need to adopt” Maxwell’s “amorphous level-of-custody rule.” He explained that the court “has always made clear that habeas is available when your claim is seeking discharge from actual physical confinement in prison to a different kind of custody,” such as a halfway house or home confinement. Here, the government relied heavily on Preiser v. Rodriguez, which held that habeas supplies the sole avenue for a state inmate to challenge the denial of credit toward release on parole.

When Gorsuch pressed Barber on the source of the government’s rule and why an inmate’s transfer to solitary confinement or maximum security would not be covered, Barber pointed principally to history and tradition in the court’s habeas cases. Barber explained, “we don’t have any tradition of claims being recognized as habeas claims challenging just transfers within prison systems.”

Despite agreeing that Maxwell could bring his claim in Section 2241, the government argued that no court could actually grant him relief. Specifically, the government pointed to 18 U.S.C. § 3621(b) and its terms barring courts from reviewing “a designation of a place of imprisonment under this subsection.” According to the government, service of a sentence in a halfway house or home confinement is “a designation of a place of imprisonment” governed by that statute.

But the government did not appear to have the votes to prevail on this argument, at least at the Supreme Court. Justice Brett Kavanaugh pressed Barber on whether that issue could be left for the lower court to decide on remand. Barber conceded that the court “absolutely could.” Sotomayor questioned Barber about whether the government is right that Section 3621(b) applies to Maxwell’s claim. But after Barber began responding, Justice Amy Coney Barrett reiterated Kavanaugh’s point that “we don’t have to get into any of this, right?” Barber again agreed.

Jackson pressed Barber on a separate point, that the BOP is expected to transfer Maxwell to a halfway house or home confinement in January 2027, which would soon make his claim moot. Jackson disputed why the court would revisit its decision to hear the case. Barber apologized for not pressing the Section 3621(b) issue or mootness in opposing certiorari, but said these factors spoke in favor of the court dismissing the case as improvidently granted.

The amicus, Brian W. Barnes, was appointed to argue in favor of the ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit that habeas is unavailable for Maxwell’s claim. When pressed by Justice Elena Kagan, Barnes agreed that habeas is available to “encompass a move from incarceration to parole,” as Preiser held. Kagan pointed out that “parole looks an awful lot like what’s going on here.”

The justices’ questions suggest that they are unlikely to limit Preiser and reject an analogy between Maxwell’s requested relief and the parole in that case. The justices also showed little appetite for reaching the government’s Section 3621(b) argument. How they would handle Maxwell’s expected release to a halfway house in January 2027 was less clear, but that circumstance could result in a speedier ruling.

Richard D. Cooke worked for the U.S. Department of Justice for 23 years, first at the Antitrust Division for 5 years and then as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia for 18 years.

#7610. Environmentalists sue to protect endangered porpoise from laxed Mexico fishing rules

In October, Mexico decreased its regulations on gillnet fishing â putting the already-critically endangered vaquita in further peril, some say.

MEXICO CITY (CN) â According to the Center for Biological Diversity, Conservation of Marine Mammals of Mexico and Greenpeace Mexico, there are only 10 vaquitas left in Baja California.

And the habitat of the small critically endangered porpoise endemic to Baja California is being threatened by the Mexican government’s newest gill net fishing regulations, they accuse in a lawsuit filed Friday.

On Oct. 14, Mexico amended a 2020 gillnet fishing regulation, reducing the prohibited gillnet fishing area and protected vaquita habitat by thousands of square miles, or by 86% of its previous area.

“The government made a decision with potentially catastrophic consequences for the vaquita without giving the public a meaningful chance to examine the proposed boundaries and respond,â said Alex Olivera, Mexico representative at the Center for Biological Diversity in a Center for Biological Diversity press release Friday.

âWith only about 10 of these little porpoises left, Mexico should be enforcing rules in the vaquitaâs entire habitat, not legalizing gillnets in waters that should be protected. Vaquitas donât follow maps, and scientists have repeatedly seen them outside the zero tolerance area.â

The environmental groups filed an amparo lawsuit, a lawsuit to pause the new regulations while the court hears the environmental groups’ case. The new environmental regulations went into effect Oct. 15, the day following the government’s amendment.

Also on Friday, in an apparent response to the lawsuit, the Mexican government issued a vow to protect the vaquita with the help of surveillance, fisheries management and combatting illegal trafficking of species with economic alternatives for coastal communities.

“The strategy links environmental conservation to social justice: protecting marine ecosystems and generating opportunities for populations that have historically depended on their natural resources. To this end, it promotes sustainable fishing and community participation in decisions on the development of the region,” the Mexican government said.

Though fishermen do not fish for vaquita, the small mammals are vulnerable to being caught in gillnets used by fishermen in Baja used to catch shrimp and illegally fish for wild totoaba.

Totoaba are an endangered fish also endemic to Baja California and are prized for their bladders known as “buche” in the Chinese black market, where they are worth hundreds of thousands of dollars.

The environmental groups claim the Mexican government failed to commit to their environmental commitments, specifically citing the the United Nations EscazÃº Agreement, which Mexico signed in September 2018.

The agreement “aims to guarantee the full and effective implementation in Latin America and the Caribbean of the rights of access to environmental information, public participation in the environmental decision-making process and access to justice in environmental matters.”

Gillnet fishing regulations have been a point of contention for environmental groups and not just recently.

In their 2017 report â one of nine lengthy reports â the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita welcomed the Mexican government’s 2017 agreement that banned commercial gillnet fishing in the Upper Gulf of Baja California but deemed it insufficient, urging a permanent and effective gillnet ban.

They argued the ban did not prohibit the sale or possession of gillnets on land and at sea in the area of the gillnet ban, leading to illegal gillnet fishing.

In response to the committee’s findings and because the vaquita are an endangered species under the U.S. Endangered Species Act, the U.S. banned the “importation of commercial fish or products from fish which have been caught with commercial fishing technology which results in the incidental kill or incidental serious injury of ocean mammals in excess of United States standards.”

#7607. Justices grapple with how to apply pretrial procedure rules in improper firing dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

How rigidly to apply the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure surfaced this week in Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, argued on Nov. 2, in which the Supreme Court addressed whether a defendant’s failure to amend its pleading and present an affirmative defense prevents that party from moving for summary judgment on the basis of that defense. To put it perhaps a bit too simply, a number of justices made clear that rules exist for a reason and should be followed.

As detailed in my preview of the case, the pretrial procedural issues arise in the context of a civil rights suit in which the plaintiff asserts that she was improperly dismissed from her job. Jasmine Younge held a high-level position in the Fulton County District Attorney’s Office for about two months until she was fired in July 2019 by District Attorney Paul Howard. Younge says she was dismissed from her job about two weeks after telling Howard that she was pregnant. Subsequently, she sued the Fulton County District Attorney’s Office for a number of civil rights violations, including the claim that she was terminated because of her pregnancy in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The DA’s office answered the complaint but never asserted in its pleadings the personal-staff exemption defense upon which it prevailed at summary judgment. (Under Title VII, certain officials are exempted from the statutory definition of employee, including members of an elected official’s “personal staff.”) Younge objected unsuccessfully to the motion, arguing as a procedural matter that it had been too late for the DA’s office to assert new affirmative defenses given that it had not amended its pleading.

Younge based her argument on Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 16(b)(4), which requires the district court to issue a pretrial scheduling order that may be modified only upon a showing of “good cause.” The pretrial scheduling order sets deadlines for the parties and, as relevant here, limits the time for parties to amend their pleadings.

Younge’s objection also was supported by Rule 15(a)(2), which sets out the standard for a litigant to amend a pleading. Under the 1962 case of Foman v. Davis, still the leading Supreme Court case on amendment under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 15(a), the court is required to consider a number of factors, including “undue delay, bad faith or dilatory motive on the part of the movant, repeated failure to cure deficiencies by amendments previously allowed, [and] undue prejudice to the opposing party by virtue of allowance of the amendment.”

The lower courts, including the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit, analyzed only whether Younge would be prejudiced by allowing the personal-staff defense to be asserted. They found that there was no prejudice and concluded on the merits that Younge was a member of the district attorney’s personal staff and therefore not covered by Title VII.

Younge successfully petitioned for review of the 11th Circuit’s judgment regarding whether amendment is required before a defendant may move for summary judgment on the basis of an unpled affirmative defense.

Eric Schnapper, an experienced Supreme Court advocate, argued on behalf of Younge at the Supreme Court. The initial questions from Justices Clarence Thomas and Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson focused on prejudice. That seems to be because even if, as Younge argued, the DA’s office did not follow Rule 15(a)(2) and amend its pleading before moving for summary judgment, the question remained: Why did the failure to amend matter when “undue prejudice” was a factor to be considered under Foman and the 11th Circuit found that Younge was not prejudiced by the DA’s failure to amend?

Yet Justice Amy Coney Barrett homed in on the core point of Younge’s argument when she stated, “going back and forth about whether you were prejudiced or not doesn't help you in your fundamental argument, which is that, procedurally, this wasn't done right.”

After several follow-up questions from Justice Elena Kagan, Schnapper responded by adopting a modest but clear position: “[T]he Court should reverse this decision, send it back, and tell the defendant if it wants to raise [an] affirmative defense to move to amend. That’s all we’re asking this Court to hold.” Over the course of the argument, his approach seemed to grow in its appeal to the justices.

Barrett also asked whether the defendant would have to file a separate motion to amend its answer or the court effectively could “construe” the defendant’s summary judgment motion as a motion to amend. She noted that the 10th Circuit has such a rule in which the court applies the standards for whether amendment is allowed without requiring the defendant to “go through the formalist exercise of actually filing a Rule 15 or 16 motion” to amend.

Schnapper did not reject the approach suggested by Barrett, commenting, “You would have to be sure to let the parties brief” whether amendment was proper. To be sure, Schnapper did not endorse the 10th Circuit’s approach. But so long as the district court is required to be asked for leave to amend, whether in a separate motion to amend or as part of a summary judgment motion, Younge would prevail in the Supreme Court because the DA’s office never sought amendment.

Several justices questioned the need for reversal and remand given the 11th Circuit’s finding that Younge had not shown prejudice by the DA office’s failure to bring this defense in its pleadings. Thomas asked what prejudice Younge suffered, commenting at one point, “I thought it was admitted that she was a member of his personal staff.” Justice Samuel Alito also seemed to resist the requirement of “a formalistic rule about filing a motion to amend for an affirmative defense.”

Stephen Petrany argued on behalf of the Fulton County DA’s office. During his argument, several justices expressed discomfort about adopting the 11th Circuit’s prejudice standard without requiring amendment. Justice Neil Gorsuch inquired about an “incredibly dilatory” affirmative defense, such as one asserted “because of reasons of bad faith,” and why that would be acceptable.

When Petrany replied that the court “has the inherent authority” to reject a summary judgment motion on that basis, Gorusch said “[t]hat seems to be an admission that Rule 15 … applies,” requiring a request to file an amended pleading so that the court can consider the conduct of the party moving for summary judgment (which may have been dilatory) as well as the actual or claimed prejudice on the nonmoving party. Shortly after that exchange, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson expressed her concern that Petrany’s position would “disincentivize parties to actually bring motions to amend.”

The court’s order granting certiorari included a question about Rule 16(b)(4), which provides that the pretrial schedule “may be modified only for good cause and with the judge's consent.” In this case, because the DA’s office moved for summary judgment after the discovery period had closed (which would have been after the deadline in the pretrial schedule for amending pleadings had passed), Younge argued that Rule 16(b)(4) applies in addition to Rule 15(a)(2), which generally governs amendment of the pleadings.

There were a number of questions about Rule 16(b)(4) during the argument, including whether it was necessary to consider this rule in order to decide the case. But the court seems likely to land where Kagan did during an exchange with Petrany: To reverse and remand the 11th Circuit with instructions to require the DA’s office to amend its answer to include the personal-staff defense and for the lower court to determine whether to allow that amendment under Rule 15(a)(2) and the factors in Foman.

Of course, it may be the case that the lower courts will allow the amendment and that the DA’s office will again prevail on its summary judgment motion. But, even if they would not have changed the ultimate outcome in this case, as Kagan put it, “The rules provide standards here. Why not just use them?” A majority of the justices seemed to agree.

Rodger D. Citron is the Associate Dean for Research and Scholarship and Professor of Law at Touro University, Jacob D. Fuchsberg Law Center.

#7606. Anthropic must face claims its Claude Max pitch misled users

A federal judge said customers could reasonably read Anthropicâs promise of â5x or 20x more usageâ as applying monthly.

(CN) â Anthropicâs promise of â5x or 20x more usageâ for its Claude Max plans could mislead customers, a federal judge in California said Friday.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Alex Tse dismissed several claims but allowed key parts of a proposed class action by Claude users to move forward.

âThe advertising in question is plausibly misleading,â Tse wrote.

But Karl Kahn and Solomon Smith, who sued on behalf of Claude Max customers, say the plans deliver far less than those promises over a full week.

For one Claude model, they calculated that Max 20x users get six times Proâs weekly usage, while Max 5x users get 3.5 times.

âI am only on my third day of the week, and I have already used 50% of my weekly allowance on the 20x Max plan,â one customer said.

Anthropic argued that customers should understand âmore usageâ to mean more usage per session, pointing to a help page that explains the limits. Tse was not persuaded.

âAnthropicâs per session disclosure is located two hyperlinks away from the primary sales pages on claude.com,â he said.

Customers did not need to visit that page to sign up, Tse said. The plaintiffs compared the disclosure to fine print on the back of a shampoo bottle. Such information may help Anthropic defend its advertising later, but it was not enough to dismiss the case at this early stage, he wrote.

Because customers pay monthly, Tse found they could reasonably understand the promise to mean five or 20 times more usage each month. An asterisk on one sales page says âUsage limits apply,â but does not mention per-session limits.

The ruling split the two plaintiffs on their claims under Californiaâs Consumers Legal Remedies Act, a law protecting consumers from deceptive business practices. The law covers purchases for personal, family or household use.

Tse found that Claude Code, the coding tool included with paid plans, could qualify as a service under the law.

Smithâs claim survived. A computer science student, he uses Claude for coursework, coding projects and an IBM-sponsored hackathon. Tse agreed that educational use does not amount to commercial use.

But Kahnâs claim did not. He said only that he uses Claude Code âto accomplish computer programming tasks,â without explaining what those tasks involve. Tse dismissed his claim but gave him a chance to provide more details.

âHe could be an entrepreneur who uses Claude Code to develop software for sale,â Tse said.

The plaintiffs can continue with claims that Anthropic negligently misrepresented its plans and broke its subscription agreements. Tse found that the contracts could include the sales pages because Anthropicâs terms point customers to âthe order processâ for details about their subscriptions.

âAnthropic didnât tighten usage limits as a bait-and-switch,â Tse said.

Representatives for Anthropic and the plaintiffs didnât immediately respond to a request for comment.

#7605. Going the Extra Mile: Jeff Xu helps dozens of New Yorkers with end-of-life needs

For nearly a decade, Jeff Xu has helped low-income New Yorkers who are 60 and older with their wills and other life planning documents through the Volunteers of Legal Service Senior Law Project.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Xu began meeting with clients over Zoom to execute these documents. He also led execution ceremonies wherever clients felt comfortable—in coffee shops, restaurants or even their homes.

For one client, Xu went all the way to Staten Island, which even as a New York City native was his first trip to its southernmost borough, he says.

“During COVID and even now, there are clients who are unable to travel, and VOLS often steers them my way because they know that I’m willing to do these types of home visits,” says Xu, a partner in the finance group at Morrison Foerster.

Abja Midha, the executive director of Volunteers of Legal Service, notes that the nonprofit organization’s staff often conducts home visits for senior clients who can’t come to the office because of physical disabilities or various medical needs. But it is far less common for pro bono attorneys to pay those calls.

“It really shows Jeff’s dedication to working with this population,” Midha says. “He will take time out of his day, traveling both ways, to meet clients in their homes to make sure they get their legal needs met. It’s truly commendable.”

Xu began handling pro bono matters for Volunteers of Legal Service when he joined Morrison Foerster as a first-year associate in 2016.

Born in Queens and raised on Long Island, Xu was surrounded by teachers and other mentors who impressed upon him the importance of community service. In high school, he volunteered at a hospital.

Later, while at Johns Hopkins University, he tutored inmates at Baltimore’s city jail.

“It was sold to me as you have to understand your privilege and your fortunate position,” says Xu, a graduate of Fordham University School of Law. “You can’t take all that for granted, and you need to pay it forward.”

As a young attorney, Xu appreciated that his firm not only encouraged but expected pro bono service. As he developed his transactional practice, he gravitated toward the Volunteers of Legal Service Senior Law Project.

He found wills, powers of attorney and advance medical directives are much like the contracts he deals with as a finance lawyer in that they must be entirely unambiguous, he says.

“There is a need for any court to look at these documents in the future and say, ‘This is exactly what’s intended. It’s totally clear. There’s no room for debate,’” Xu says. “That parallels nicely with my day-to-day.”

Xu has since helped dozens of clients finalize their wishes for end-of-life care and the disposition of their assets. As part of the process, he arranges initial meetings with clients in person, over the phone or remotely. After preparing their documents, he meets with them again for the execution ceremony.

Xu says he often needs to be flexible and creative. During home visits, he asks clients to enlist their friends and neighbors as witnesses. He also finds ways to communicate with clients who may not have reliable access to a phone or email.

In one instance during the pandemic, Xu received a card from a woman that included $60. Even though he returned the money, he felt like he made a real difference by settling her affairs and relieving her worries.

“Frankly, that’s why I keep doing this,” Xu says. “As people are approaching the end of their life, a lot of them don’t have the means to pay for an attorney, and they’re intimidated by what it takes to do it yourself. They’re stuck in this weird spot where they just don’t do anything.”

Jennifer Brown, supervising counsel of pro bono at Morrison Foerster, describes Xu as a “very willing volunteer.” By her last count, he had provided more than 750 hours of pro bono service.

Because of his relationship with Volunteers of Legal Service, the nonprofit once asked Xu to assist with a training for Morrison Foerster attorneys, Brown recalls.

It was an unusual request, and what Xu told his colleagues was striking, she adds.

“He said it might be scary, the idea of talking to people about these issues, because they’re very personal, and they can call up a lot for people,” Brown says. “He was so sensitive, and it was clear that he doesn’t see these matters as, you know, ‘We’ll just fill out this collection of forms for someone.’”

After Xu was promoted to partner last year, he took a more active role in recruiting and training other lawyers at Morrison Foerster to represent clients through the Volunteers of Legal Service Senior Law Project.

While Xu handles three or four of his own matters annually, he oversees attorneys in his group and in other groups at the firm who are handling countless more, he says.

“That’s the number that’s really more important, because I am able to encourage other attorneys to get involved with this, and then hopefully that multiplies in a way that is positive,” Xu says.

Xu expanded his work with Volunteers of Legal Service in other ways, including by organizing execution clinics at the firm so multiple clients can finalize their life planning documents at one time. He also joined its board of directors and is working more on fundraising.

“Those types of things are where my mind is at, in terms of what I’m trying to do pro bono-wise,” says Xu, who received the New York State Bar Association’s President’s Pro Bono Service Award for the First Judicial District for his work in May. “Those are the things I will continue to do.”

Apart from his focus on pro bono, Xu, whose parents emigrated from China, encourages diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives in his firm. He lives on Long Island with his wife and 3-year-old daughter, with whom he spends the rest of his time.

“But before I had a 3-year-old, and during the pandemic, I got really into baking bread,” adds Xu, who often gifted loaves to colleagues and clients. “It got to the point where my wife was like, ‘You have to slow this down.’”

Members Who Inspire is an ABA Journal series profiling exceptional ABA members. If you know members who do unique and important work, you can nominate them for this series by emailing [email protected].

#7600. DOJ steps up its investigation into the Dobbs leak

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

This week, during the first half of the November argument session, the justices heard oral arguments in four cases and quickly declined a request from the Trump administration to intervene in a voting dispute in California. However, headlines about these developments were overshadowed by Tuesday’s midterm elections. The blue wave brought new significance to debates over court reform and when Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas might retire.

Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied two requests for a stay of execution from Jesse Guardado, who was sentenced to death for the 2004 murder of Jackie Malone. Hours later, Guardado was executed in Florida.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review. Here is the link to our Case Preview.

On Tuesday, the justices heard argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

On Monday, the justices heard argument in Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

The justices also heard argument on Monday in Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis.

Monday morning, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by individuals who it contends are noncitizens. Just hours later, the court denied the request. There were no noted dissents.

Later on Monday, the court released its calendar for the January argument session, which will begin on Monday, Jan. 11.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the court to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request has been fully briefed since last Friday, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Looking ahead, the justices will hear arguments on Monday in two cases: Nielsen v. Watanabe, on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations; and Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc., on whether the “just compensation” paid to land owners losing property to a pipeline project should be determined by referring to state law, which often provides for a higher payment than what the Constitution requires.

Jodi Kantor and Michael S. Schmidt, The New York Times

In May 2022, Politico released a leaked draft of the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned the right to abortion. The leak was “a seismic breach of confidentiality” and led to “an internal inquiry by the court,” although “no leaker has ever been publicly identified.” But The New York Times reported on Thursday that the Justice Department is now “pursuing a criminal investigation into who leaked” the draft opinion and that this “investigation has ramped up in recent weeks as prosecutors have sent grand jury subpoenas for testimony and sought information from people who worked at the court at the time of the leaks.”

On Thursday, defenders of “a Cook County, Illinois, ordinance that makes it unlawful to sell or possess any ‘assault weapon or large capacity magazine,’ including AR-15 rifles,” asked the Supreme Court to dismiss a challenge to the ban that’s set to be argued in December, Viramontes v. Cook County. Attorneys for Cook County contended that the case is now moot after the “lead plaintiff, Cutberto Viramontes, asked [on Oct. 29] to be removed from the litigation without explanation.” Although the filings represent “a puzzling twist” in the case, “whether Viramontes is permitted to withdraw would have limited practical significance for the broad question of whether state and local governments may ban AR-15-style rifles,” according to CNN. That’s because Viramontes was consolidated with another case on a similar law in Connecticut, “which would continue even if the Supreme Court decided to dismiss the Cook County litigation. And whatever the court decides on Connecticut’s ban would almost certainly affect whether other bans like the one in Cook County can stand.”

Tuesday’s midterm elections “all but guaranteed” President Donald Trump won’t be able to put a fourth justice on the Supreme Court. Beginning in January, Democrats will have “a Senate majority—with a several-seat cushion—that will make it easy to block Trump judicial nominees, especially for any Supreme Court vacancies that might arise in 2027 or 2028,” according to The Wall Street Journal. Faced with this reality, “[s]ome legal observers have floated a last-ditch scenario in which [Clarence] Thomas or [Samuel] Alito could announce their retirement in the coming days and give Trump and the outgoing Republican Senate a chance to quickly install a successor before the newly elected Congress is seated on Jan. 3.” But the Journal described this scenario as “exceedingly unlikely,” in large part because neither Alito nor Thomas appears interested in retiring. And it’s not “clear that a Supreme Court nominee could get through the lame-duck Congress even if there were a retirement, especially because some moderate Republican senators are on their way out of office and blame Trump for losing their seats.”

In a Thursday interview with the Associated Press, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said “that Democrats will not allow President Donald Trump to put ‘a right-winger’ on the Supreme Court once they take power.” He “would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until after the next presidential election, as former Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. But he said that Democrats are ‘not going to allow any crappy nominees’ to be confirmed to the Supreme Court.” “The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer said.

In a column for Bloomberg, Noah Feldman contended that Tuesday’s election results “should cause Democrats to reconsider the wisdom of plans to pack the court or strip it of jurisdiction over certain issues.” It should no longer feel as urgent to make such changes, according to Feldman, because “[i]f a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028 and the Democrats hold the Senate, the Democrats will have a chance to flip the court from 6-3 conservative to 5-4 liberal” simply by filling predicted or expected vacancies. The reform proposals floated in recent months “make little sense if Democrats take seriously the prospect of a liberal recapture of the institution,” Feldman wrote.

The Supreme Court heard argument on Monday in Maxwell v. Dinis on whether a federal inmate may use a habeas statute to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem: Does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers?

In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman offered an in-depth analysis of Justice Elena Kagan, examining not only how she votes, but also how she chooses to agree and disagree.

In her Ratio Decidendi column, Stephanie Barclay revisited Tuesday’s argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, noting that the discussion put a spotlight on 1990’s Employment Division v. Smith, a controversial ruling that made it easier for the government to overcome free exercise challenges. The ruling in St. Mary, according to Barclay, “will determine how much is left of” Smith, which has already fallen out of favor with the court.

In his Relist Watch column on Wednesday, John Elwood explored four petitions for review that will get a second look from the justices at today’s conference. Three concern a long-running dispute over Alabama’s congressional districts and the fourth asks whether using a car makes an otherwise local kidnapping a federal crime – even when the car never crosses a state line.

In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky explored Nielsen v. Watanabe, in which the court is considering under what circumstances federal officers may be sued for money damages for constitutional violations, noting that the case comes at a time when efforts “to hold ICE agents accountable” have taken on new urgency.

On Oct. 19, the Supreme Court granted review in Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education, a case on race and school admissions. In his AV Ristorante column on Monday, Brian Fitzpatrick explained why he believes “it could be the final nail in affirmative action’s coffin.”

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the Texas Supreme Court’s blue wave, the possibility of a majority-Democrat Supreme Court, and one of the biggest Supreme Court cases of the term: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice Peter V. Daniel, who served on the court from 1841/2 to 1860.

Like some of the other justices we’ve covered, Justice Peter V. Daniel is one that “[f]ew recall or have ever heard of.” Those who know of Daniel have not been complimentary. He has been called “a brooding proslavery fanatic” according to law professor Earl Maltz, and a 1965 book review likened him to the notoriously bigoted Justice James C. McReynolds, minus McReynolds’ occasional “charm.”

Daniel was born in April 1784 on his family’s estate in Stafford County, Virginia. After studying with private tutors and a brief stint at the College of New Jersey (now Princeton University), he read law in Richmond under Edmund Randolph, President George Washington’s attorney general and secretary of state. In 1810, Daniel married Randolph’s daughter, Lucy.

In November 1808, Daniel fought a duel in Maryland against businessman John Seddon; Seddon later died from his injuries. This did not appear to significantly slow Daniel’s career, however: He subsequently spent two one-year terms in the Virginia House of Delegates, a tenure his biographer, John P. Frank, judged as “utterly undistinguished.” In 1812, Daniel joined Virginia’s Council of State, which advised the governor, and from 1818 to 1835 served as lieutenant governor. His “friends” “apparently lacked any real warmth or affection for him, complaining of his ‘frozen deportment,’” which played out literally: In the winter of 1813, Daniel reportedly balked at spending a modest sum to keep militiamen warm, despite their officer’s warning that the men’s lives were at stake, on the reasoning that Virginia state law made the soldiers responsible for their own clothing.

Daniel’s Richmond law practice was modestly successful, but he had other aspirations. Through the Richmond Junto (a Virginia Democratic-Republican network) he organized and led the state’s Jacksonians, and, along with then-New York governor Martin Van Buren, built an “Albany-Richmond axis,” which backed Andrew Jackson for president. Daniel subsequently turned down Jackson’s offer of attorney general. In 1836, however, he accepted a federal judgeship in eastern Virginia, Jackson’s reward for his party loyalty and his support for the president’s war on the national bank.

When Justice Philip Barbour died in February 1841, Van Buren had roughly a week left in office and rushed to nominate Daniel to the court. Aware of Daniel’s reputation, Whig senators tried to stall the vote, at one point walking out together to leave the chamber without a quorum, while Democratic leaders searched the capital for their own absent senators. Daniel was ultimately confirmed 22-5 in a midnight vote. The exact date he took the oath is unclear; the Federal Judicial Center lists it in January 1842 “based on questionable authority,” while one biography entry has him joining the court in December 1841.

After he joined the bench, Daniel’s circuit assignment included Arkansas and Mississippi, which involved arduous trips from Washington. While circuit riding in 1851, for example, Daniel rode in a canal boat for two days to get from D.C. to Pittsburgh (and was not a fan of the other “vulgar and filthy” passengers).

On the court itself, close to one in three of Daniel’s written opinions was a dissent, and during his tenure, his solo dissents outnumbered any other justice’s by more than two to one. He fought against extending federal admiralty power to inland waters, and when the court did just that in 1852’s Genesee Chief v. Fitzhugh, Daniel was the lone dissenter. Perhaps his best-known majority opinion came in 1848’s West River Bridge Co. v. Dix, which put Daniel opposite the famed lawyer and statesman Daniel Webster. Daniel detested Webster so much that, after meeting him, he reported his hand “was actually contaminated by contact with his.” In the case, Vermont had taken over a privately chartered toll bridge, paid compensation, and opened it as a free road, but the bridge company argued that the takeover breached the contract clause of the Constitution. Writing for the majority, Daniel held that the franchise was ordinary property that the state could take through eminent domain.

Daniel, who was a slaveholder, concurred in 1842’s Prigg v. Pennsylvania, which held that the federal Fugitive Slave Act preempted Pennsylvania’s ban on recapturing formerly enslaved persons. After Van Buren joined the antislavery Free Soilers, Daniel’s friendship with him ended, and Daniel reportedly swore he would never again set foot north of Maryland (he came to blame even bad weather on the North). In Dred Scott v. Sandford, Daniel argued that freed slaves could not be citizens because they had once been held as property and that the Northwest Ordinance of 1787 (which, among many other things, had kept slavery out of land north and west of the Ohio River) was unconstitutional, thus taking a more extreme position than even Chief Justice Roger Taney, who wrote the majority opinion.

Daniel’s first wife, Lucy, died in 1847, and his second wife died in 1857 after a candle accidentally lit her clothes on fire. Daniel died in Richmond in May 1860 following a lengthy illness. In February 1861, Republican senators blocked President James Buchanan’s pick to replace him, Jeremiah Black, making the seat one of the three vacancies that President Abraham Lincoln filled in 1862. It stayed open until July 1862, when Lincoln chose Justice Samuel Miller.

In a December 1860 memorial, the attorney general said that Daniel “held the pen of a ready writer,” but “was sometimes in danger of going too directly to his purpose and treating with too much contempt the obstacles that intervened.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?”

MR. SCHEPERS: “In our view, Atkins was new at the time it was decided.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “We're talking about now, though.”

MR. SCHEPERS: “That – we believe that Atkins was new based off of the character of the decision in 2002 and that it remains new now.”

JUSTICE THOMAS: “What about Marbury v. Madison?”

As ballots continue to be counted in Mississippi's Senate race, Democrat Scott Colom's candidacy has taken on historic significance for Black voters in the state.

JACKSON, Miss. (AP) â Democrat Scott Colom hasn’t won Mississippiâs U.S. Senate race, but the local prosecutor was welcomed as a historic figure Friday as he strolled through the Farish Street business district where civil rights leaders once organized.

âItâs so wonderful! Itâs so wonderful to have Scott Colom as our representative,â said Maati Jone Primm, who owns Marshallâs Music & Bookstore in Jackson.

The state is still tallying ballots that could make Colom the first Black senator from this Deep South state since post-Civil War Reconstruction. The possibility of Colom defeating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith puts many Black voters somewhere between cautious optimism and outright celebration in a state where nearly 40% of the population is Black but the top representation for generations has been white.

âIâm so glad we are at the point where we are,â said Sorie Tarawally, a 76-year-old attorney who has long known Colomâs father. He called the 43-year-old candidate âthe man, our messiah, our savior.â

The contest remains too early for The Associated Press to call, and Colomâs historic bid will hinge on a tedious process playing out in elections offices across Mississippiâs 82 counties. Local officials are receiving and examining absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots, before deadlines next week. Volunteers and lawyers representing each campaign look on in anticipation of potential litigation.

âWeâre going to make sure everything is followed according to the law, and I have confidence in those local officials,â Colom said. âTheyâre doing their jobs. Got to be patient with them.â

Colom said ballots tallied since Tuesday’s election lean in his favor, and he chided Hyde-Smith for not explaining her strategy going forward.

âSheâs still our senator. Where is she? Why is she not doing any interviews?â Colom asked. âWhy canât she explain what her pathway to success is?"

Hyde-Smith has not appeared publicly since election night, when she essentially declared victory despite a razor-thin margin with ballots still uncounted.

“We are not backing down,” she posted Friday on social media. âThis election is not over. Our team is working across Mississippi to monitor the remaining ballots and protect the integrity of the process. We will see this through to the very end!â

The pool of outstanding ballots includes absentee ballots, which can be counted in Mississippi as long as they are received by Tuesday, five business days after the election. The rest are affidavit ballots, which are cast at the polls when there’s a glitch: Perhaps the person’s name was not on the rolls or the person did not have proper identification, or a poll worker determined the person’s identification did not precisely match the name on the list.

Citizens who had identification issues have until Tuesday to address those matters in person at their local elections office. For people who were not on a precinctâs rolls, local officials can verify a person’s status using previous records and information on the affidavit that person filed when filling out a ballot. That person typically has no responsibility to come to a local elections office; ballot status can be found on the Mississippi secretary of stateâs office website.

Counties have until Friday to certify complete results to the secretary of state.

Mississippi law has no provision for a statewide recount. Campaigns could seek court orders, usually county by county, seeking to examine ballots.

Democrats already have won control of the Senate, so the result in Mississippi would not change the balance of power in Washington.

But it would mark a seismic shift in the state, where white conservatives have dominated the Statehouse and congressional delegation for nearly 150 years. Through Jim Crow segregation and the Civil Rights era, those leaders were nearly all Democrats. After the Civil Rights Movement, they overwhelmingly shifted to Republicans. For Black Mississippians, the result was the same: a lack of proportional representation at the top levels of state government and in Washington.

Colom was initially viewed as a long shot, and it wasn’t until late October that Senate Democrats’ top campaign group started spending on advertising to support him. But the midterms revealed a broad backlash against redistricting efforts in the South that were aimed at boosting Republicans and, by extension, reducing Black representation.

Primm’s bookstore, where Colom visited on Friday, opened in the 1930s and is recognized as the oldest Black-owned bookstore in the U.S.

She said the Farish Street neighborhood still represents Black Mississippiansâ âfirst migration, from the plantation to the city.â Having Colom there as a potential senator âmakes us so proud, and it gives us someone to aspire to. Our youth need to see the possibilities for their lives, and we do when we see our next senator from Mississippi.â

As he campaigned, Colom emphasized that he can represent all Mississippians, and he said President Donald Trumpâs policies â the war with Iran and tariffs, especially â cut across all demographic lines. He even celebrated the extended ballot counting process as a benefit to the state’s 2.95 million residents.

âIâm so glad the national press is getting to see the beauty of our state,â he said.

But Colom and his Black supporters also have never ignored the significance of his candidacy as a Black man.

âWe are motivated by the gross inequalities we have seen in society and how only one side seems to benefit,â said Tarawally, who was born in Sierra Leone and arrived in the Deep South to attend law school at the University of Mississippi. âSo, we want a person who speaks to our benefit.â

Colom ended his campaign with an ad set at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who was gunned down in 1963 in his own driveway, dying in front of his wife and children.

âItâs a powerful reminder of the sacrifice to gain the ballot, and nobody sacrificed more than Medgar Evers and his family,â Colom said Friday.

âWhat was important to me about that ad is we didnât ask people to vote for me. We just talked about the sacrifice, talked about the story,â he continued. âWe just wanted that to be the closing ad because I wanted that to be the last message that the people of Mississippi heard.â

#7595. Democrats won control of Congress. So what does that mean for the Supreme Court?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Democrats won big in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping at least 40 seats in the House and at least seven in the Senate. Come January, the Democratic Party will control both houses of Congress, which will allow it to set policymaking priorities and play a lead role in shaping the future of the Supreme Court.

Most immediately, the power shift in the Senate will complicate (if not effectively eliminate) President Donald Trump’s ability to appoint another justice to the Supreme Court, should a vacancy arise after the new Congress is seated. The Democratic Party will have enough votes to reject a nomination – if it even allows confirmation hearings to proceed.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7592. The poisoned public rights doctrine and Sun Valley Orchards

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On Tuesday, Nov. 10, the court will hear argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC. This case concerns the H-2A visa program for temporary alien immigrant workers. The issue is whether the Department of Labor’s Article II administrative law judges have the authority to collect ruinous fines from employers who violate their employment contracts with such individuals.

In early August of this year, I signed an amicus brief supporting Sun Valley Orchards along with former Attorneys General Edwin Meese III and Michael Mukasey and law professor Gary Lawson, prepared and filed by our lawyer Amit Vora. We argued that the respondent was entitled not only to a Seventh Amendment civil jury but also to an Article III federal court.

After reading the government’s opening and reply briefs by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, I stand by our argument that a DOL administrative law judge may not deprive Sun Valley of property by imposing ruinous fines for violating a contract that bound it to follow certain labor laws in employing foreign immigrant H-2A workers. Rather, Sun Valley has a Seventh Amendment right to have its claims heard by a jury if it desires to do so.

The government is obviously correct that the government has a sovereign right to control immigration into the United States under the H-2A program. It does not follow from that, however, that the government can condition the admission of foreign workers under this program on Sun Valley’s surrendering its constitutional right to have employment disputes with those workers adjudicated by Article III courts with a Seventh Amendment right to a jury trial. Constitutional rights cannot be taken away without due process of law or in violation of, for example, the First, Fourth, or Seventh amendments. But that is exactly what the government is trying to do in this case.

By way of example, in 1987’s Nollan v. California Coastal Commission, the Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Antonin Scalia, held that the California Coastal Commission could not use its plenary power over zoning to condition a renovation construction permit on the Nolans ceding a public easement to walk along their valuable California coastal property, as doing so would violate the takings clause of the Fifth Amendment. Likewise, the government cannot impose unconstitutional conditions when using either its zoning power or its plenary power over immigration. Nor can the government use its commerce power or any of its other enumerated powers to violate one’s constitutional rights. The government can shut down the foreign immigrant H2A program. But it cannot use it as a cudgel to make Americans surrender their constitutional rights simply because the rights of immigrants are at stake.

Central to the government’s argument otherwise is the public-rights doctrine. This doctrine – properly understood – allows for privileges created by the government to be adjudicated by non-Article III judges, such as the privileges to receive social-security, disability, or welfare payments; the privilege to immigrate into the United States; or the privilege to receive tax rebates under the federal government’s partial waiver of sovereign immunity. With regard to such privileges, the Constitution’s guarantee of an Article III forum and the Seventh Amendment civil jury trial right are inapplicable because the receipt of these were not property rights recognized at common law, but privileges created by the government. The government argues that because immigration into the country is also a privilege, not a right, Sun Valley’s conduct related to this are not subject to Article III protections.

It is true that the public rights doctrine was profoundly altered (one could say poisoned), in the 1977 case of Atlas Roofing Co. v. Occupational Safety and Health Administration. In Atlas Roofing, Justice Byron White denied access to an Article III court and a Seventh Amendment civil jury trial to a party subject to an OSHA enforcement order. According to White, because such orders were based on “new statutory obligations,” they could be “committed exclusively to an administrative agency [for] deciding whether a violation has in fact occurred.” This was incorrect: while OSHA created new torts that can occur in the workplace, these were analogous to the kinds of tort actions that would have been heard at common law. Indeed, such torts are classic “Cases in Law,” which Article III gives sole jurisdiction over to life-tenured federal judges assisted by a civil jury if the plaintiffs choose one. Thus, Atlas Roofing Co. changed the law to say that the public-rights doctrine not only allowed Article II administrative law judges to deprive persons of privileges, but, for the first time, it also eliminated the guarantee of a Seventh Amendment jury trial when a person or entity was deprived of property rights by the government.

Fortunately, this dangerous precedent was limited by the more recent 2024 case of SEC v. Jarkesy. In Jarkesy, the Supreme Court held that when the SEC imposed civil penalties against a defendant for securities fraud, the Seventh Amendment entitled the defendant to a jury trial. This is because in 1787 a fraud case, like the employment contract case at issue in Sun Valley (or, for that matter, the property seized in Atlas Roofing), would have been “Case in Law” assigned to the sole jurisdiction of the Article III courts.

So the lesson of Jarkesy is this: While the vast majority of cases which ALJs decide only “privileges” and not “rights” only require an Article II hearing, when federal regulatory agencies impose ruinous fines on a corporation or person, those fines are deprivations of one’s right to property. And in depriving one of such property, it is not enough to have an administrative hearing: The case must be heard by an Article III court with the right to a Seventh Amendment civil-jury trial.

The public-rights doctrine then does not apply to enforcement orders that deprive a person of property by agencies such as OSHA in Atlas Roofing, the SEC in Jarkesy, or the DOL in Sun Valley. Nor does calling a case an immigration matter empower the government to take away the constitutional rights of Americans even if immigration into the United States is itself a privilege and not a right.

So let’s hope that the Supreme Court in Sun Valley rejects, as unconstitutional, the DOL’s attempt to funnel a private-rights dispute away from an Article III forum. And let’s further hope that the court clearly reframes the public-rights doctrine, as limited in Jarkesy, as a mere manifestation of the rights/privileges distinction – and continues to prevent the doctrine from taking the form that Justice White allowed for in Atlas Roofing: an ominous threat to Article III, the Seventh Amendment, and the due process clause.

Professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

#7589. Justices consider when a constitutional rule is “previously unavailable” to prisoner

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about whether a Texas man on death row can bring a second federal post-conviction challenge to his sentence by arguing that, under updated psychiatric standards, he was found intellectually disabled and therefore cannot be executed.

Except in a few narrow circumstances, the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 bars prisoners from filing a petition for federal post-conviction relief challenging the grounds for their detention when an earlier petition has already been rejected. One of these exceptions is when such a claim relies on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The other is if facts “underlying the [initial] claim” would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable fact finder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

In 2007, Dexter Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. Five years before his conviction, the Supreme Court held in Atkins v. Virginia that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment. A defense expert at Johnson’s trial concluded that, under the diagnostic standards employed at the time, Johnson was not intellectually disabled. Following his conviction, Johnson filed an initial habeas petition and invoked Atkins to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.

In May 2013, while Johnson’s first federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the DSM-5, a new edition of its diagnostic manual that deemphasized IQ cutoffs. Texas’ highest criminal court adopted this in 2018. In 2019, Johnson scored 70 on an IQ test, and an expert concluded he met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability. Johnson then filed a successive habeas challenge in the district court claiming that he could not be executed under Atkins. The trial court subsequently ruled that his claim (based on the later diagnostic criteria) had been “previously unavailable,” and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed that decision. The 5th Circuit denied rehearing, and Texas came to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

At oral argument, Texas Solicitor General William Peterson told the justices that Congress “chose to allow new claims in these applications only in limited circumstances that do not include changes in the diagnostic standards for intellectual disability.” There is no “new rule” “previously unavailable” here, because Atkins was decided before Johnson “even committed his crimes,” Peterson said.

Justice Elena Kagan pressed Peterson on why the DSM “isn’t … part of the law?” She suggested that the DSM-5 effectively created “a kind of Atkins I and an Atkins II” – first, a rule barring the execution of people with intellectual disabilities, followed by a “substantive standard” defining what it means to be intellectually disabled. Kagan later described the Atkins standard as akin to a rule with a “big gap in it” where “the DSM comes and plugs it in and it becomes part of the legal standard.”

The justices further debated what it means for a rule to be “available.” Kagan suggested, based on prior precedent, that something is “not available to you” if it makes you “run into a brick wall.” “[I]f I was going to be [previously] laughed out of court,” she said, “then, really, the rule was unavailable to me.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told Peterson that, as she understood AEDPA, Congress’ “policy choice was to give individuals one clear shot at bringing their constitutional claims.” Under Texas’ interpretation, she said, “Mr. Johnson will never get that opportunity,” which “seems like a really incongruous consequence.”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for her part, suggested that the outcome should turn on something like ripeness (whether a case is sufficiently developed for a court to decide). As she remarked to Peterson, “[i]f what we have said under Atkins is you cannot execute someone who is mentally ill, we have a certain way of determining that, and it doesn't become ripe until the DM-5 makes it ripe.”

Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked Peterson whether the court “could resolve this case solely on the new rule issue without addressing ‘previously unavailable.’” Peterson said it could, but that Texas was asking the court to decide the “previously unavailable” question.

On behalf of Johnson, Jeremy Schepers told the justices that “existence and availability aren’t the same thing.” Atkins existed, but Johnson’s claim – based on the change in diagnostic criteria – was not previously available. When the clinical standards for intellectual disability change, Schepers argued, “the Eighth Amendment’s protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time.”

Justice Clarence Thomas was skeptical, asking, “Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?” Schepers responded that Atkins “remains new now.” “What about Marbury v. Madison?” Thomas responded. Justice Amy Coney Barrett noted that when “Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone, that was new.” But “I don't think anybody would describe the telephone as new today.”

Kavanaugh pointed Schepers to a “friend of the court” brief filed by Louisiana and 21 other states, which argued that because the medical standards are “constantly evolving,” Johnson’s position is “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality.” Schepers said that was incorrect, because a state prisoner gets “one opportunity to raise any claim,” and “so a prisoner could not raise a second Atkins claim.”

At one point, Justice Samuel Alito asked about a future edition of the DSM that “makes smaller changes” that “provide a greater opportunity for success.” Schepers said that claim would fail under the 5th Circuit’s reading, because “[i]t’s only a question of whether the claim had a possibility of merit before.”

Emily Ferguson, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued as a “friend of the court” in support of Texas, emphasized that it is “difficult to imagine Congress enacting a law that would allow the American Psychiatric Association, without independent action of this Court, to create a new rule of constitutional law.” She also noted that the court had made clear “states would be responsible for the method of determining intellectual disability,” and it would then make little “sense for there to be an available successive application anytime the relevant state had a new … supreme court case … or even a state lower court case that changed the framework that the state was using.”

Alito asked Ferguson whether the “Atkins rule” was “that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that is regarded as such by medical professionals,” or if “it is that a person may not be executed if the person has an intellectual disability that can't be justified by the recognized purposes of punishment,” for which “the DSM would be evidence but not part of the standard itself?” Ferguson responded that the “latter formulation captures what … the Atkins Eighth Amendment rule was.”

Perhaps the most noticeable takeaway from oral argument was how subdued the justices were. The chief justice did not ask any questions, and no justice appeared to take up Johnson’s request in his brief that the court dismiss the case as improvidently granted (that is, decide that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and not resolve it), as the court did last term in Hamm v. Smith, another Atkins case.

A decision is expected by late June but is likely to come earlier.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7588. Supreme Court agrees to weigh in on Goldman Sachs arbitration dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Friday afternoon added a new case to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term, granting a petition for review filed by Goldman Sachs Bank in a case over whether and when a bankruptcy court can override the Federal Arbitration Act and refuse to honor an agreement to arbitrate disputes.

The dispute in which the justices agreed to weigh in, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown, began three years ago, when Rhea Brown and Gregory Maze filed for bankruptcy. Both listed credit card debts with Goldman Sachs Bank as one of their debts.

The Bankruptcy Code imposes an automatic stay, which (among other things) bars creditors from attempting to collect debts from someone who has filed for bankruptcy. Because Goldman Sachs, according to Maze and Brown, repeatedly continued to try to seek payment of their credit card debts, they filed an adversary proceeding (that is, a separate lawsuit within the broader bankruptcy case) against the bank, in which they contended that the bank had willfully violated the automatic stay provision.

Pointing to an arbitration clause in their credit card agreements, Goldman Sachs asked the bankruptcy court to put the adversary proceeding on hold and require Brown and Maze to arbitrate their dispute. The bankruptcy court denied that request, and both the federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld that ruling. A divided three-judge panel of the 4th Circuit concluded that requiring Brown and Maze to arbitrate their claim “would interfere and conflict with the strong and established policies and purposes of the Bankruptcy Code.”

Goldman Sachs came to the Supreme Court in June, asking the justices to take up its case. It told the court that the 4th Circuit’s ruling squarely conflicted with a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit. Moreover, it added, “[t]he practical stakes of these issues are enormous” because of the ubiquity of arbitration clauses in consumer credit agreements. The 4th Circuit’s decision, it said, “imperils the enforceability of arbitration agreements in many of them.”

After considering Goldman Sachs’ petition for review at four consecutive conferences, the justices granted it on Friday afternoon. The case likely will be argued sometime next year, with a decision to follow by late June or early July.

More orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday are expected at 9:30 a.m. EST on Monday.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.
